**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), used through the Fourier-coefficient suppliers. Fix $N\ge1$, a real viscosity parameter $\nu\ge0$ and a real exponent $s>3/2$. Work in the notation of [[def-periodic-vector-sobolev-space-and-leray-projection]]: $H^s=H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ with coefficients $\widehat u(k)$, weights $w_k$, Leray projection $P$, differential operators $\partial_j,\Delta$ and divergence-free subspace $H^s_\sigma$.

**Definitions.** For a coefficient family $c$ let $(P_Nc)(k):=c(k)$ if $|k|_\infty\le N$ and $(P_Nc)(k):=0$ otherwise (\emph{Fourier truncation}); let
$$X_N:=\{\,u\in H^0:\widehat u(k)=0\ \text{for }|k|_\infty>N,\ k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0\ \forall k,\ \widehat u(-k)=\overline{\widehat u(k)}\ \forall k\,\}$$
be the space of real divergence-free trigonometric-polynomial fields of frequency at most $N$, and define the **Galerkin field**
$$F_N:X_N\longrightarrow H^0,\qquad F_N(u):=-P_NP\bigl((u\cdot\nabla)u\bigr)+\nu\Delta u .$$

Then:

1. $X_N$ is a finite-dimensional real-linear subspace of $H^s$ for every $s\in\mathbb R$, $P_N$ restricted to the real divergence-free subspace $H^s_\sigma$ is the orthogonal projection onto $X_N$ for the $H^s$ inner product and $\|P_Nu\|_{H^s}\le\|u\|_{H^s}$; moreover $F_N$ maps $X_N$ into $X_N$, and $\int_{\mathbb T^3}F_N(u)\,dx=0$ and $F_N(P_Nu)=F_N(u)$ for $u\in X_N$.
2. **Local Lipschitz property.** For every $R>0$ there is $L_N(R)<+\infty$ such that $\|F_N(u)-F_N(v)\|_{H^s}\le L_N(R)\|u-v\|_{H^s}$ whenever $u,v\in X_N$ with $\|u\|_{H^s},\|v\|_{H^s}\le R$; the proof exhibits $L_N(R)=12\pi^2\nu N^2+6C_sc_NR$ with $c_N=(1+12\pi^2N^2)^{1/2}$ and $C_s$ the product constant of [[lem-discrete-young-and-sobolev-product]].
3. **Galerkin IVP.** For every $u_0\in X_N$ the initial value problem
$$u'(t)=F_N(u(t)),\qquad u(0)=u_0$$
has a unique maximal solution $u_N:I\to X_N$ with open interval $I\ni0$; if the maximal interval has finite right endpoint $T_{\max}<+\infty$, then $\lim_{t\uparrow T_{\max}}\|u_N(t)\|_{H^{s'}}=+\infty$ for every $s'>3/2$, and conversely if $\|u_N\|_{H^{s'}}\le R$ on $[0,T)$ for some $s'>3/2$ with $T<+\infty$ then the solution extends past $T$. For $u_0\in H^0_\sigma$ arbitrary, $P_Nu_0\in X_N$ and the corresponding solution is written $u_N(\cdot;P_Nu_0)$.
4. **Basic bounds.** Along the maximal solution:
   (a) for every real $m>3/2$,
   $$\|u_N'(t)\|_{H^m}\le\nu\|u_N(t)\|_{H^{m+2}}+3C_m\|u_N(t)\|_{H^{m+1}}^2 ,$$
   where $C_m$ is the product constant of [[lem-discrete-young-and-sobolev-product]] at order $m$;
   (b) for every real $0\le m\le2$, with $c_N=(1+12\pi^2N^2)^{1/2}$ and $e_N=(1+48\pi^2N^2)^{1/2}$,
   $$\|u_N'(t)\|_{H^m}\le12\pi^2\nu N^2\|u_N(t)\|_{H^m}+3C_sc_Ne_N^2\|u_N(t)\|_{H^s}^2 ;$$
   (c) $\|P_Nu-u\|_{H^r}\le(2\pi(N+1))^{-1}\|u\|_{H^{r+1}}$ for every real $r$ and every $u\in H^{r+1}$.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), used through the Fourier-coefficient suppliers. Fix $N\ge1$, $\nu\ge0$ and a real $s>5/2$, and let $u_N:I\to X_N$ be the maximal solution of the Galerkin system $u_N'=F_N(u_N)$ of [[lem-fluid-galerkin-coefficient-ivp]] with initial datum $u_N(0)=P_Nu_0$, where $u_0\in H^s_\sigma$ and $Y_0:=\|u_0\|_{H^s}$.

1. **Energy inequality.** For every real $m\ge s$ and every $t\in I$,
$$\frac12\frac{d}{dt}\|u_N(t)\|_{H^m}^2+\nu\|\nabla u_N(t)\|_{H^m}^2\;\le\;C_m\|u_N(t)\|_{H^s}\|u_N(t)\|_{H^m}^2 ,$$
where $C_m$ is the commutator constant of [[lem-tame-transport-commutator]] (claim 2), and $\|\nabla u_N\|_{H^m}^2:=\sum_{j=1}^3\|\partial_ju_N\|_{H^m}^2$.
2. **Common lifespan.** With
$$T:=\begin{cases}(2C_sY_0)^{-1},&Y_0>0,\\ 1,&Y_0=0,\end{cases}$$
one has $[0,T]\subseteq I$ and
$$\|u_N(t)\|_{H^s}\le2Y_0\quad(0\le t\le T);$$
if $Y_0=0$ then $u_N\equiv0$ on $I$. In particular the same interval length $T$, depending only on $Y_0$ and $s$ (and not on $N$ or on the finer profile of $u_0$), is a common interval of existence for all Galerkin approximations.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix $N\ge1$, $\nu\ge0$, a real $s>5/2$, and $u_0\in H^s_\sigma$ with $Y_0=\|u_0\|_{H^s}$, and let $T$ and $u_N:[0,T]\to X_N$ be as in [[lem-fluid-energy-common-lifespan]]. For every real $m\ge s$ with $\|u_0\|_{H^m}<+\infty$ define
$$B_m:=\|u_0\|_{H^m}\,e^{4C_mY_0T},\qquad B_m':=\nu B_m+3C_{m-2}B_{m-1}^2 ,$$
where $C_m$ is the commutator constant of [[lem-tame-transport-commutator]] and $3C_{m-2}$ is the product constant of [[lem-discrete-young-and-sobolev-product]] at order $m-2$ (so that $B_m'$ is defined for $m>7/2$). For lower orders $0\le r<s$ set $B_r:=B_s$; then $\|u_N(t)\|_{H^r}\le B_r$ follows from monotonicity of the weights and the base bound. At any order where an initial norm is infinite, take $B_r=+\infty$ and the corresponding $B_r\prime=+\infty$ by convention, reading the estimate as an extended upper bound. Then for $0\le t\le T$:

1. $\|u_N(t)\|_{H^m}\le B_m$ for every real $m\ge s$; in particular all bounds hold on the single interval $[0,T]$ whose length depends only on $Y_0$ and $s$, uniformly in $N$.
2. $\|u_N'(t)\|_{H^{m-2}}\le B_m'$ for every real $m>7/2$; in particular, for the integer orders of the main theorem ($s\ge4$, $m\ge s$) these are the uniform-in-$N$ bounds on $L^\infty(0,T;H^m)$ and $L^\infty(0,T;H^{m-2})$ of the Galerkin approximations.

Fix $N\ge1$, a real viscosity parameter $\nu\ge0$ and a real exponent $s>3/2$. For $u_0\in H^0_\sigma$ arbitrary, $P_Nu_0\in X_N$ and the corresponding solution is written $u_N(\cdot;P_Nu_0)$.
4. **Basic bounds.** Along the maximal solution:
   (a) for every real $m>3/2$,
   $$\|u_N'(t)\|_{H^m}\le\nu\|u_N(t)\|_{H^{m+2}}+3C_m\|u_N(t)\|_{H^{m+1}}^2 ,$$
   where $C_m$ is the product constant of [[lem-discrete-young-and-sobolev-product]] at order $m$;
   (b) for every real $0\le m\le2$, with $c_N=(1+12\pi^2N^2)^{1/2}$ and $e_N=(1+48\pi^2N^2)^{1/2}$,

   (c) $\|P_Nu-u\|_{H^r}\le(2\pi(N+1))^{-1}\|u\|_{H^{r+1}}$ for every real $r$ and every $u\in H^{r+1}$.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), used through the two lattice and embedding suppliers quoted below. Use the scalar and vector spaces and weights of [[def-periodic-vector-sobolev-space-and-leray-projection]]. For scalar $a,b$ put $ab$ equal to ordinary multiplication; for scalar $a$ and vector $v$ put $av=(av_1,av_2,av_3)$; for vectors $v,z$ put $vz=(v_1z_1,v_2z_2,v_3z_3)$ (componentwise product). These products extend complex-bilinearly to coefficients and satisfy $|ab|\le|a||b|$, with Euclidean norm for vectors and absolute value for scalars. The output is scalar only for two scalar inputs, and vector otherwise. The convolution for the same typed products is $(a*b)(k):=\sum_l a(l)b(k-l)$ whenever the sum is absolutely convergent. In claim 3, $f,g$ are vector fields and $f\cdot\nabla$ denotes the explicitly displayed scalar-component action, not componentwise vector multiplication.

1. **Discrete Young.** Let $a\in\ell^1(\mathbb Z^3;\mathbb C)$, $b\in\ell^2(\mathbb Z^3;\mathbb C)$ and define $(a*b)(k):=\sum_{l\in\mathbb Z^3}a(k-l)b(l)$. The sum converges absolutely, and
$$\|a*b\|_{\ell^2}\;\le\;\|a\|_{\ell^1}\|b\|_{\ell^2}.$$
2. **Sobolev product.** Let $\sigma>3/2$ and let $f,g$ each belong to its scalar or vector $H^\sigma$. Then the pointwise product $fg$ of the continuous representatives ([[lem-fourier-lattice-sobolev-embedding]]) belongs to $H^\sigma$, and with $W_\sigma=(\sum_kw_k^{-2\sigma})^{1/2}$ of [[lem-cm-lattice-shell-count-and-weight-sums]],
$$\|fg\|_{H^\sigma}\;\le\;C_\sigma\|f\|_{H^\sigma}\|g\|_{H^\sigma},\qquad C_\sigma:=2^\sigma W_\sigma .$$
3. **Transport product.** Let $\sigma>3/2$, $f\in H^\sigma$ and $g\in H^{\sigma+1}$. Then $(f\cdot\nabla)g:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}f_j\,\partial_jg$ belongs to $H^\sigma$ and
$$\|(f\cdot\nabla)g\|_{H^\sigma}\;\le\;3C_\sigma\|f\|_{H^\sigma}\|g\|_{H^{\sigma+1}}.$$

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), which is used by the imported Fourier-basis theorem quoted below.

**The three-torus and its measure.** Let $\mathbb T:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the one-dimensional torus with its quotient topology and its normalized Haar integral $m_{\mathbb T}$ ([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]); $\mathbb T$ is compact Hausdorff ([[lem-finite-tori-are-compact-hausdorff-character-spaces]]). Put $\mathbb T^3:=\mathbb T\times\mathbb T\times\mathbb T$ with the finite product topology. Let $dx:=m_{\mathbb T}\otimes m_{\mathbb T}\otimes m_{\mathbb T}$ be the product measure on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb T^3$ ([[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]], [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]); being a product of probability measures it is a probability measure. For a vector $k=(k_1,k_2,k_3)\in\mathbb Z^3$ and $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in\mathbb T^3$ define the **character**
$$e_k(x):=\exp\bigl(2\pi i\,(k_1x_1+k_2x_2+k_3x_3)\bigr)=e^{2\pi i\,k\cdot x},$$
where each $x_j$ is inserted through any real representative and $\exp$ is the complex exponential ([[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]); the definition does not depend on the representatives. Then $|e_k(x)|=1$, $e_k e_l=e_{k+l}$, and $e_{-k}=\overline{e_k}$.

**Function spaces.** Write $L^2:=L^2(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ for the real Hilbert space of (equivalence classes of) real Borel vector fields $u:\mathbb T^3\to\mathbb R^3$ with $\int_{\mathbb T^3}|u|_2^2\,dx<+\infty$, inner product $\langle u,v\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb T^3}u\cdot v\,dx$ and norm $|u|_2:=\langle u,u\rangle^{1/2}$; here $u\cdot v$ is the Euclidean inner product of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Similarly $L^1(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb C^3)$ denotes the integrable complex vector fields.

**Fourier coefficients.** For $u\in L^1(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb C^3)$ and $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ define
$$\widehat u(k):=\int_{\mathbb T^3}u(x)\,e_{-k}(x)\,dx\ \in\mathbb C^3 .$$
The integral depends only on the class of $u$. A field $u\in L^1$ is real almost everywhere if and only if $\widehat u(-k)=\overline{\widehat u(k)}$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z^3$; the forward direction uses $\widehat{\overline u}(k)=\overline{\widehat u(-k)}$, and the reverse uses $L^1$ Fourier uniqueness, proved below. On the circle this uniqueness follows from [[thm-fejer-convergence-in-lp]] with $p=1$: zero coefficients give zero Fejer means, whose $L^1$ limit is the function. To pass to $\mathbb T^d$ for $d=2,3$, use [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: for fixed $k'\in\mathbb Z^{d-1}$, $g_{k'}(x_1)=\int_{\mathbb T^{d-1}}u(x_1,x')e_{-k'}(x')dx'$ is in $L^1(\mathbb T)$ and all its coefficients vanish. Hence $g_{k'}=0$ almost everywhere. The countable union of the exceptional sets over $k'$ is null. For every remaining $x_1$, the $L^1$ section in $x'$ has all coefficients zero, so induction in $d$ makes it zero almost everywhere. Fubini then makes $u=0$ almost everywhere on $\mathbb T^d$. Apply this uniqueness to $u-\overline u$ to obtain the reverse real-valuedness implication. For $u\in L^2\subset L^1$ (finite measure) the coefficient map is the one of the imported theorem, which states: $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}$ is an orthonormal basis of the complex Hilbert space $L^2(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb C)$, the finite-subset-net expansion $u=\sum_k\widehat u(k)e_k$ and the Parseval identities hold, and $u\mapsto\widehat u$ is a surjective linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb C)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^3;\mathbb C)$ ([[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]]); the last statement applied componentwise gives $\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_k\widehat u(k)\cdot\overline{\widehat v(k)}$ for real $u,v\in L^2$.

**Weights.** For $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ set
$$w_k:=\bigl(1+|2\pi k|_2^2\bigr)^{1/2}=\bigl(1+4\pi^2|k|_2^2\bigr)^{1/2}\ \ge 1,$$
so that $w_k\ge|2\pi k_j|$ for $j=1,2,3$ and $w_{k+l}\le w_k+w_l$ for all $k,l\in\mathbb Z^3$.

**The coefficient space and $H^s$.** For $s\in\mathbb R$ let $\ell^2_s$ be the complex Hilbert space of all $c:\mathbb Z^3\to\mathbb C^3$ with
$$\|c\|_{\ell^2_s}^2:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}w_k^{2s}|c(k)|_2^2<+\infty,\qquad \langle c,d\rangle_{\ell^2_s}:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}w_k^{2s}\,c(k)\cdot\overline{d(k)} ,$$
and let $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}:=\{c\in\ell^2_s: c(-k)=\overline{c(k)}\ \forall k\}$. The set $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$ is closed in $\ell^2_s$ and is a real-linear subspace; on it the Hermitian pairing $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\ell^2_s}$ is real valued, because the substitution $k\mapsto-k$ shows that it equals its own conjugate. By the imported theorem the coefficient map restricts to a bijection of the set of real classes of $L^2$ onto $\ell^2_{0,\mathbb R}$. For $s\ge0$ define
$$H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3):=\{u\in L^2:\widehat u\in\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}\},\qquad \|u\|_{H^s}:=\|\widehat u\|_{\ell^2_s}.$$
For $s<0$ define $H^s$ to be the completion of the real trigonometric polynomials in the same weighted coefficient norm, equivalently the space of formal real coefficient families $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$. For an element of this completion $\widehat u(k)$ means its coefficient, not an integral of an assumed $L^2$ function. The embedding of $L^2$ into these negative-order spaces is its coefficient map. Truncation makes finite families dense, so this completion is all of $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$, not merely the coefficient families of $L^2$ fields. Consequently each $H^s$ is a real Hilbert space isometric to $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$ through $u\mapsto\widehat u$, and $\|u\|_{H^0}=|u|_2$. If $s\ge t$ then $H^s\subseteq H^t$ and $\|u\|_{H^t}\le\|u\|_{H^s}$. The **trigonometric polynomials** are the fields $p=\sum_{k\in F}c_k e_k$ with $F\subseteq\mathbb Z^3$ finite and $c_{-k}=\overline{c_k}$ (equivalently, real coefficient families of finite support); they belong to every $H^s$, and the finitely supported families are dense in each $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$ (truncate a family to $|k|_\infty\le M$ and let $M\to\infty$), so trigonometric polynomials are dense in every $H^s$.

**Scalar spaces.** For $s\in\mathbb R$ define $\ell^2_s(\mathbb Z^3;\mathbb C)$ to consist of families $c:\mathbb Z^3\to\mathbb C$ with $\sum_k w_k^{2s}|c(k)|^2<\infty$, with pairing $\sum_k w_k^{2s}c(k)\overline{d(k)}$; its real subspace is specified by $c(-k)=\overline{c(k)}$. For $s\ge0$, $H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R)$ consists of real scalar $L^2$ classes with this weighted coefficient norm; for $s<0$ it is the completion of real scalar trigonometric polynomials, identified with the real coefficient subspace. Scalar Fourier coefficients are $\widehat f(k)=\int f e_{-k}\,dx$ when $f\in L^1$, and otherwise denote the completion coordinates. Parseval and truncation give the scalar Hilbert-space and density assertions exactly as above. A vector belongs to $H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ exactly when each of its three scalar components belongs to $H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R)$, with $\|u\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{j=1}^3\|u_j\|_{H^s}^2$. Below the value type distinguishes scalar and vector $H^s$; $\Lambda^s$, $\partial_j$ and $\Delta$ have the same multipliers for scalars, $\nabla$ maps scalar to vector spaces, and $\operatorname{div}$ maps vector to scalar spaces.

**The operators $\Lambda^s$, $\partial_j$, $\Delta$, $\nabla$ and $\operatorname{div}$.**
For $s,t\in\mathbb R$ and $u\in H^t$ define $\Lambda^s u\in H^{t-s}$ by the coefficient rule
$$\widehat{\Lambda^s u}(k):=w_k^{s}\,\widehat u(k);$$
then $\Lambda^s$ is a linear isometric isomorphism of $H^t$ onto $H^{t-s}$, $\Lambda^0=\mathrm{id}$, $\Lambda^s\Lambda^t=\Lambda^{s+t}$, and $\Lambda^{-s}$ is the inverse of $\Lambda^s$. For $j=1,2,3$ and $u\in H^{s+1}$ define $\partial_j u\in H^s$ by
$$\widehat{\partial_j u}(k):=2\pi i\,k_j\,\widehat u(k);$$
for $u\in H^{s+2}$ define $\Delta u\in H^s$ by $\widehat{\Delta u}(k):=-4\pi^2|k|_2^2\,\widehat u(k)$; for a scalar field $f$ with coefficients $\widehat f(k)\in\mathbb C$ in the scalar spaces just defined, define $\nabla f\in H^s$ for $f\in H^{s+1}$ by $\widehat{\nabla f}(k):=2\pi i\,k\,\widehat f(k)$; and for $u\in H^{s+1}$ define $\operatorname{div}u:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j u_j\in H^s$. These operators satisfy $\|\partial_j u\|_{H^s}\le\|u\|_{H^{s+1}}$, $\|\Delta u\|_{H^s}\le\|u\|_{H^{s+2}}$, and for every integer $m\ge1$, $\Lambda^{2m}=(I-\Delta)^m$, the identity following coefficientwise from $w_k^2=1+4\pi^2|k|_2^2$. On trigonometric polynomials all four operators agree with the classical coordinatewise derivatives and divergence computed from the smooth functions $x\mapsto e^{2\pi ik\cdot x}$, by the classical rules $\partial_j e_k=2\pi i k_j e_k$; this is the convention in which the notation is used below.

**Divergence-free fields and the Leray projection.** For $s\in\mathbb R$ put
$$H^s_\sigma(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3):=\bigl\{\,u\in H^s: k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0\ \text{for every }k\in\mathbb Z^3\,\bigr\};$$
this is a closed real-linear subspace of $H^s$, and $\operatorname{div}u=0$ in $H^s$ for $u\in H^{s+1}_\sigma$. For $k\neq0$ let $\pi_k\in L(\mathbb C^3)$ be the orthogonal projection onto the hyperplane $\{k\}^\perp$,
$$\pi_k v:=v-\frac{k\cdot v}{|k|_2^2}\,k ,$$
and set $\pi_0:=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C^3}$. Define the **Leray projection** $P$ by
$$\widehat{Pu}(k):=\pi_k\widehat u(k)\qquad(k\in\mathbb Z^3).$$
Then: $P$ maps $H^s$ linearly into $H^s_\sigma$, and $\|Pu\|_{H^s}\le\|u\|_{H^s}$; $P^2=P$; $P$ is self-adjoint on $H^s$, i.e. $\langle Pu,v\rangle_{H^s}=\langle u,Pv\rangle_{H^s}$ for all $u,v\in H^s$; $P$ commutes with each $\Lambda^t$, with each $\partial_j$, and with $\Delta$ wherever these are defined; and the identity $\operatorname{div}(Pu)=0$ holds in $H^{s-1}$ for $u\in H^s$. Moreover every $u\in H^s$ has the orthogonal decomposition
$$u=Pu+\nabla f,\qquad f\in H^{s+1},\quad \widehat f(0)=0,\qquad \langle Pu,\nabla f\rangle_{H^s}=0.$$
Here zero mean means zero coefficient at $0$ (the usual integral when the field is integrable); orthogonality for all real orders is in the $H^s$ pairing. The scalar element $f$ is determined by $\widehat f(0):=0$ and $\widehat f(k):=\dfrac{k\cdot\widehat u(k)}{2\pi i\,|k|_2^2}$ for $k\neq0$; here $f\in H^{s+1}$ because $w_k^{2(s+1)}|\widehat f(k)|^2\le C\,w_k^{2s}|\widehat u(k)|^2$ for $k\neq0$, and $\widehat{\nabla f}(k)=\bigl(k\cdot\widehat u(k)/|k|_2^2\bigr)k=\widehat u(k)-\pi_k\widehat u(k)$. In particular $P\nabla f=0$ for every $f$ with $\nabla f\in H^s$, so $P$ is the orthogonal projection of $H^s$ onto $H^s_\sigma$. On smooth fields the decomposition $u=Pu+\nabla f$ derived above from the Fourier coefficients is called the Hodge decomposition of the torus; the operator $P$ is the Leray projection of the fluid literature.

**Time-dependent fields.** For an interval $[0,T]$ with $T>0$ and $s\in\mathbb R$, let $C([0,T],H^s)$ denote the set of continuous maps from $[0,T]$ to the metric space $(H^s,\|\cdot\|_{H^s})$, with $\|u\|_{C([0,T],H^s)}:=\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|u(t)\|_{H^s}$. For a map $u:[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^\infty$ we mean that every mixed partial derivative $\partial_t^r\partial_x^\alpha u$ exists and is continuous on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3$, with one-sided time derivatives at $t=0,T$.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), used through the Fourier-coefficient suppliers. Fix $N\ge1$, a real viscosity parameter $\nu\ge0$ and a real exponent $s>3/2$. Work in the notation of [[def-periodic-vector-sobolev-space-and-leray-projection]]: $H^s=H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ with coefficients $\widehat u(k)$, weights $w_k$, Leray projection $P$, differential operators $\partial_j,\Delta$ and divergence-free subspace $H^s_\sigma$.

**Definitions.** For a coefficient family $c$ let $(P_Nc)(k):=c(k)$ if $|k|_\infty\le N$ and $(P_Nc)(k):=0$ otherwise (\emph{Fourier truncation}); let
$$X_N:=\{\,u\in H^0:\widehat u(k)=0\ \text{for }|k|_\infty>N,\ k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0\ \forall k,\ \widehat u(-k)=\overline{\widehat u(k)}\ \forall k\,\}$$
be the space of real divergence-free trigonometric-polynomial fields of frequency at most $N$, and define the **Galerkin field**
$$F_N:X_N\longrightarrow H^0,\qquad F_N(u):=-P_NP\bigl((u\cdot\nabla)u\bigr)+\nu\Delta u .$$

Then:

1. $X_N$ is a finite-dimensional real-linear subspace of $H^s$ for every $s\in\mathbb R$, $P_N$ restricted to the real divergence-free subspace $H^s_\sigma$ is the orthogonal projection onto $X_N$ for the $H^s$ inner product and $\|P_Nu\|_{H^s}\le\|u\|_{H^s}$; moreover $F_N$ maps $X_N$ into $X_N$, and $\int_{\mathbb T^3}F_N(u)\,dx=0$ and $F_N(P_Nu)=F_N(u)$ for $u\in X_N$.
2. **Local Lipschitz property.** For every $R>0$ there is $L_N(R)<+\infty$ such that $\|F_N(u)-F_N(v)\|_{H^s}\le L_N(R)\|u-v\|_{H^s}$ whenever $u,v\in X_N$ with $\|u\|_{H^s},\|v\|_{H^s}\le R$; the proof exhibits $L_N(R)=12\pi^2\nu N^2+6C_sc_NR$ with $c_N=(1+12\pi^2N^2)^{1/2}$ and $C_s$ the product constant of [[lem-discrete-young-and-sobolev-product]].
3. **Galerkin IVP.** For every $u_0\in X_N$ the initial value problem
$$u'(t)=F_N(u(t)),\qquad u(0)=u_0$$
has a unique maximal solution $u_N:I\to X_N$ with open interval $I\ni0$; if the maximal interval has finite right endpoint $T_{\max}<+\infty$, then $\lim_{t\uparrow T_{\max}}\|u_N(t)\|_{H^{s'}}=+\infty$ for every $s'>3/2$, and conversely if $\|u_N\|_{H^{s'}}\le R$ on $[0,T)$ for some $s'>3/2$ with $T<+\infty$ then the solution extends past $T$. For $u_0\in H^0_\sigma$ arbitrary, $P_Nu_0\in X_N$ and the corresponding solution is written $u_N(\cdot;P_Nu_0)$.
4. **Basic bounds.** Along the maximal solution:
   (a) for every real $m>3/2$,
   $$\|u_N'(t)\|_{H^m}\le\nu\|u_N(t)\|_{H^{m+2}}+3C_m\|u_N(t)\|_{H^{m+1}}^2 ,$$
   where $C_m$ is the product constant of [[lem-discrete-young-and-sobolev-product]] at order $m$;
   (b) for every real $0\le m\le2$, with $c_N=(1+12\pi^2N^2)^{1/2}$ and $e_N=(1+48\pi^2N^2)^{1/2}$,
   $$\|u_N'(t)\|_{H^m}\le12\pi^2\nu N^2\|u_N(t)\|_{H^m}+3C_sc_Ne_N^2\|u_N(t)\|_{H^s}^2 ;$$
   (c) $\|P_Nu-u\|_{H^r}\le(2\pi(N+1))^{-1}\|u\|_{H^{r+1}}$ for every real $r$ and every $u\in H^{r+1}$.

Let $X$ be a real vector space ([[def-vector-space]]) with a norm $\|\cdot\|$ ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]) whose metric $d(x,y):=\|x-y\|$ is complete ([[def-complete-metric-space]]). Let $a<b$ be reals ([[def-interval]]) and let $g:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). For endpoints $c,d\in[a,b]$, set $\int_c^c g:=0_X$ and, when $c>d$, set $\int_c^d g:=-\int_d^c g$; for $c<d$ use the Riemann-sum construction below on the restriction to $[c,d]$. Then:

1. **Integral.** For every sequence of tagged partitions of $[a,b]$ whose mesh tends to $0$, the Riemann sums $\sum_i(t_{i+1}-t_i)\,g(s_i)$ converge in $X$; the limit, written $\int_a^b g$, is independent of the sequence, and
$$\Bigl\|\int_a^b g\Bigr\|\;\le\;(b-a)\sup_{t\in[a,b]}\|g(t)\| .$$
2. **Fundamental theorem.** The curve $G:[a,b]\to X$, $G(t):=\int_a^t g$, is well defined, satisfies $\|G(t)-G(s)\|\le(t-s)\sup_{[s,t]}\|g\|$ for $a\le s\le t\le b$, and is differentiable with $G'=g$ on $[a,b]$ in the one-sided sense at the endpoints.
3. **Linearity.** For continuous $g,h:[a,b]\to X$ and reals $\alpha,\beta$: $\int_a^b(\alpha g+\beta h)=\alpha\int_a^b g+\beta\int_a^b h$; and for $a\le c\le b$, $\int_a^b g=\int_a^c g+\int_c^b g$.
4. **Bounded linear images.** If $Y$ is a normed real vector space and $T:X\to Y$ is linear with $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for some $C<+\infty$ and all $x$, then $T\circ g$ is continuous and $T\bigl(\int_a^b g\bigr)=\int_a^b (T\circ g)$; in particular, for every real-linear functional $\Lambda:X\to\mathbb R$ with $|\Lambda x|\le C\|x\|$, $\Lambda\bigl(\int_a^b g\bigr)=\int_a^b\Lambda\circ g$.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\nu\ge0$, let $T>0$, and let $u:[0,T]\to\bigcap_{p\in\mathbb R}H^p(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ be a curve such that, in the notation of [[def-periodic-vector-sobolev-space-and-leray-projection]]:

1. for every real $p$, $t\mapsto u(t)$ is continuous into $H^p$;
2. for every real $p$, $t\mapsto u(t)$ is differentiable into $H^p$, with
$$u'(t)=\nu\Delta u(t)-P\bigl((u(t)\cdot\nabla)u(t)\bigr)\qquad(0\le t\le T),$$
the right-hand side being an element of $H^p$ for every $p$ (which follows from the other hypotheses as below);
3. $u(t)$ is divergence-free and real for every $t$.

Then the map $(t,x)\mapsto u(t,x)$ belongs to $C^\infty([0,T]\times\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ (with one-sided time derivatives at the endpoints). For every integer $r\ge0$ and spatial multi-index $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)\in\mathbb N_0^3$, with $\partial_x^\alpha:=\partial_1^{\alpha_1}\partial_2^{\alpha_2}\partial_3^{\alpha_3}$, one has $\partial_t^r\partial_x^\alpha u=\partial_x^\alpha\Phi_r$, where $\Phi_0:=u$ and, for integers $r\ge1$,
$$\Phi_r:=\nu\Delta(\partial_t^{r-1}u)-P\!\left(\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}\binom{r-1}{j}\bigl(\partial_t^ju\cdot\nabla\bigr)\partial_t^{r-1-j}u\right).$$
Thus for $r\ge1$ the identity uses $r-1$ differentiations of the equation for $u'$, while $r=0$ is the spatial derivative of $u$ itself.

boundaries.evidence: The local-fluid Statement uses the fixed three-torus, the cutoff sequence and the nonempty real Sobolev-order range. Step 1.1 constructs a limit of that sequence, rather than an empty Galerkin family.
Statement clause 3 and step 5.1 include zero initial norm with T=1 and zero solution. The nu=0 branch is the Euler model and remains covered in step 2.1.
The local-fluid construction includes cutoff N=1 and any one-mode smooth divergence-free initial field. Step 1.1 invokes the uniform estimates for every positive cutoff.

Step 1.1 uses divergence-free Galerkin fields, satisfying the conditional divergence-free conclusion of the compactness supplier. Step 2.1 uses the correct truncation of projected nonlinear fields and one additional Sobolev derivative in its tail bound.

The local-fluid Statement provides a solution on the closed interval through T, with one-sided endpoint derivatives from the bootstrap. The explicit time formula excludes division by zero via the separately stated zero-data branch.

boundaries.reason: The local-fluid Statement declares countable choice. Its compactness supplier now constructs the diagonal deterministically; the field is obtained from those convergent coefficients, with no independent selections of solutions by time.
The local-fluid theorem asserts a sufficient local existence construction and estimates; it makes no equivalence between those conditions and global regularity.
The local-fluid existence claim supplies no converse from a smooth observed field to the adopted Euler or viscous model. Its conclusions are conditional deductions from the stated equations.

risk_review.notes: All-order smooth initial norms feed the common base lifespan and derivative bounds; deterministic diagonal extraction converges in every chosen H^m. Nonlinearity converges by splitting its two bilinear differences and cutoff tail; viscous convergence explicitly uses extraction one order higher to control Delta in H^(m-2). Finite-dimensional componentwise FTC proves the Galerkin integral equation; uniform norm convergence passes its integral to the limit, with zero-length convention at t=0. For target H^p choose integer m≥max(s+1,p+2), so the established equation in H^(m-2) licenses differentiation in H^p. Bootstrap yields joint smoothness, coefficient zero-mode convergence preserves mean, and zero datum gives zero solution. No stronger global or empirical assertion is inferred.

citations.quote:
**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), which is used by the imported Fourier-basis theorem quoted below.

**The three-torus and its measure.** Let $\mathbb T:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the one-dimensional torus with its quotient topology and its normalized Haar integral $m_{\mathbb T}$ ([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]); $\mathbb T$ is compact Hausdorff ([[lem-finite-tori-are-compact-hausdorff-character-spaces]]). Put $\mathbb T^3:=\mathbb T\times\mathbb T\times\mathbb T$ with the finite product topology. Let $dx:=m_{\mathbb T}\otimes m_{\mathbb T}\otimes m_{\mathbb T}$ be the product measure on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb T^3$ ([[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]], [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]); being a product of probability measures it is a probability measure. For every remaining $x_1$, the $L^1$ section in $x'$ has all coefficients zero, so induction in $d$ makes it zero almost everywhere. Fubini then makes $u=0$ almost everywhere on $\mathbb T^d$. $$\pi_k v:=v-\frac{k\cdot v}{|k|_2^2}\,k ,$$

$$\widehat{Pu}(k):=\pi_k\widehat u(k)\qquad(k\in\mathbb Z^3).$$

In claim 3, $f,g$ are vector fields and $f\cdot\nabla$ denotes the explicitly displayed scalar-component action, not componentwise vector multiplication.

1. **Discrete Young.** Let $a\in\ell^1(\mathbb Z^3;\mathbb C)$, $b\in\ell^2(\mathbb Z^3;\mathbb C)$ and define $(a*b)(k):=\sum_{l\in\mathbb Z^3}a(k-l)b(l)$. The sum converges absolutely, and
$$\|a*b\|_{\ell^2}\;\le\;\|a\|_{\ell^1}\|b\|_{\ell^2}.$$
2. **Sobolev product.** Let $\sigma>3/2$ and let $f,g$ each belong to its scalar or vector $H^\sigma$. Then the pointwise product $fg$ of the continuous representatives ([[lem-fourier-lattice-sobolev-embedding]]) belongs to $H^\sigma$, and with $W_\sigma=(\sum_kw_k^{-2\sigma})^{1/2}$ of [[lem-cm-lattice-shell-count-and-weight-sums]],
$$\|fg\|_{H^\sigma}\;\le\;C_\sigma\|f\|_{H^\sigma}\|g\|_{H^\sigma},\qquad C_\sigma:=2^\sigma W_\sigma .$$
3. **Transport product.** Let $\sigma>3/2$, $f\in H^\sigma$ and $g\in H^{\sigma+1}$. Then $(f\cdot\nabla)g:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}f_j\,\partial_jg$ belongs to $H^\sigma$ and
$$\|(f\cdot\nabla)g\|_{H^\sigma}\;\le\;3C_\sigma\|f\|_{H^\sigma}\|g\|_{H^{\sigma+1}}.$$

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), which is used by the imported Fourier-basis theorem quoted below.

**The three-torus and its measure.** Let $\mathbb T:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the one-dimensional torus with its quotient topology and its normalized Haar integral $m_{\mathbb T}$ ([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]); $\mathbb T$ is compact Hausdorff ([[lem-finite-tori-are-compact-hausdorff-character-spaces]]). Put $\mathbb T^3:=\mathbb T\times\mathbb T\times\mathbb T$ with the finite product topology. Let $dx:=m_{\mathbb T}\otimes m_{\mathbb T}\otimes m_{\mathbb T}$ be the product measure on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb T^3$ ([[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]], [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]); being a product of probability measures it is a probability measure. For a vector $k=(k_1,k_2,k_3)\in\mathbb Z^3$ and $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in\mathbb T^3$ define the **character**
$$e_k(x):=\exp\bigl(2\pi i\,(k_1x_1+k_2x_2+k_3x_3)\bigr)=e^{2\pi i\,k\cdot x},$$
where each $x_j$ is inserted through any real representative and $\exp$ is the complex exponential ([[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]); the definition does not depend on the representatives. Then $|e_k(x)|=1$, $e_k e_l=e_{k+l}$, and $e_{-k}=\overline{e_k}$.

**Function spaces.** Write $L^2:=L^2(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ for the real Hilbert space of (equivalence classes of) real Borel vector fields $u:\mathbb T^3\to\mathbb R^3$ with $\int_{\mathbb T^3}|u|_2^2\,dx<+\infty$, inner product $\langle u,v\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb T^3}u\cdot v\,dx$ and norm $|u|_2:=\langle u,u\rangle^{1/2}$; here $u\cdot v$ is the Euclidean inner product of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Similarly $L^1(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb C^3)$ denotes the integrable complex vector fields.

**Fourier coefficients.** For $u\in L^1(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb C^3)$ and $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ define
$$\widehat u(k):=\int_{\mathbb T^3}u(x)\,e_{-k}(x)\,dx\ \in\mathbb C^3 .$$
The integral depends only on the class of $u$. A field $u\in L^1$ is real almost everywhere if and only if $\widehat u(-k)=\overline{\widehat u(k)}$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z^3$; the forward direction uses $\widehat{\overline u}(k)=\overline{\widehat u(-k)}$, and the reverse uses $L^1$ Fourier uniqueness, proved below. On the circle this uniqueness follows from [[thm-fejer-convergence-in-lp]] with $p=1$: zero coefficients give zero Fejer means, whose $L^1$ limit is the function. To pass to $\mathbb T^d$ for $d=2,3$, use [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: for fixed $k'\in\mathbb Z^{d-1}$, $g_{k'}(x_1)=\int_{\mathbb T^{d-1}}u(x_1,x')e_{-k'}(x')dx'$ is in $L^1(\mathbb T)$ and all its coefficients vanish. Hence $g_{k'}=0$ almost everywhere. The countable union of the exceptional sets over $k'$ is null. For every remaining $x_1$, the $L^1$ section in $x'$ has all coefficients zero, so induction in $d$ makes it zero almost everywhere. Fubini then makes $u=0$ almost everywhere on $\mathbb T^d$. Apply this uniqueness to $u-\overline u$ to obtain the reverse real-valuedness implication. For $u\in L^2\subset L^1$ (finite measure) the coefficient map is the one of the imported theorem, which states: $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}$ is an orthonormal basis of the complex Hilbert space $L^2(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb C)$, the finite-subset-net expansion $u=\sum_k\widehat u(k)e_k$ and the Parseval identities hold, and $u\mapsto\widehat u$ is a surjective linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb C)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^3;\mathbb C)$ ([[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]]); the last statement applied componentwise gives $\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_k\widehat u(k)\cdot\overline{\widehat v(k)}$ for real $u,v\in L^2$.

**Weights.** For $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ set
$$w_k:=\bigl(1+|2\pi k|_2^2\bigr)^{1/2}=\bigl(1+4\pi^2|k|_2^2\bigr)^{1/2}\ \ge 1,$$
so that $w_k\ge|2\pi k_j|$ for $j=1,2,3$ and $w_{k+l}\le w_k+w_l$ for all $k,l\in\mathbb Z^3$.

**The coefficient space and $H^s$.** For $s\in\mathbb R$ let $\ell^2_s$ be the complex Hilbert space of all $c:\mathbb Z^3\to\mathbb C^3$ with
$$\|c\|_{\ell^2_s}^2:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}w_k^{2s}|c(k)|_2^2<+\infty,\qquad \langle c,d\rangle_{\ell^2_s}:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}w_k^{2s}\,c(k)\cdot\overline{d(k)} ,$$
and let $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}:=\{c\in\ell^2_s: c(-k)=\overline{c(k)}\ \forall k\}$. The set $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$ is closed in $\ell^2_s$ and is a real-linear subspace; on it the Hermitian pairing $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\ell^2_s}$ is real valued, because the substitution $k\mapsto-k$ shows that it equals its own conjugate. By the imported theorem the coefficient map restricts to a bijection of the set of real classes of $L^2$ onto $\ell^2_{0,\mathbb R}$. For $s\ge0$ define
$$H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3):=\{u\in L^2:\widehat u\in\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}\},\qquad \|u\|_{H^s}:=\|\widehat u\|_{\ell^2_s}.$$
For $s<0$ define $H^s$ to be the completion of the real trigonometric polynomials in the same weighted coefficient norm, equivalently the space of formal real coefficient families $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$. For an element of this completion $\widehat u(k)$ means its coefficient, not an integral of an assumed $L^2$ function. The embedding of $L^2$ into these negative-order spaces is its coefficient map. Truncation makes finite families dense, so this completion is all of $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$, not merely the coefficient families of $L^2$ fields. Consequently each $H^s$ is a real Hilbert space isometric to $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$ through $u\mapsto\widehat u$, and $\|u\|_{H^0}=|u|_2$. If $s\ge t$ then $H^s\subseteq H^t$ and $\|u\|_{H^t}\le\|u\|_{H^s}$. The **trigonometric polynomials** are the fields $p=\sum_{k\in F}c_k e_k$ with $F\subseteq\mathbb Z^3$ finite and $c_{-k}=\overline{c_k}$ (equivalently, real coefficient families of finite support); they belong to every $H^s$, and the finitely supported families are dense in each $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$ (truncate a family to $|k|_\infty\le M$ and let $M\to\infty$), so trigonometric polynomials are dense in every $H^s$.

**Scalar spaces.** For $s\in\mathbb R$ define $\ell^2_s(\mathbb Z^3;\mathbb C)$ to consist of families $c:\mathbb Z^3\to\mathbb C$ with $\sum_k w_k^{2s}|c(k)|^2<\infty$, with pairing $\sum_k w_k^{2s}c(k)\overline{d(k)}$; its real subspace is specified by $c(-k)=\overline{c(k)}$. For $s\ge0$, $H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R)$ consists of real scalar $L^2$ classes with this weighted coefficient norm; for $s<0$ it is the completion of real scalar trigonometric polynomials, identified with the real coefficient subspace. Scalar Fourier coefficients are $\widehat f(k)=\int f e_{-k}\,dx$ when $f\in L^1$, and otherwise denote the completion coordinates. Parseval and truncation give the scalar Hilbert-space and density assertions exactly as above. A vector belongs to $H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ exactly when each of its three scalar components belongs to $H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R)$, with $\|u\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{j=1}^3\|u_j\|_{H^s}^2$. Below the value type distinguishes scalar and vector $H^s$; $\Lambda^s$, $\partial_j$ and $\Delta$ have the same multipliers for scalars, $\nabla$ maps scalar to vector spaces, and $\operatorname{div}$ maps vector to scalar spaces.

**The operators $\Lambda^s$, $\partial_j$, $\Delta$, $\nabla$ and $\operatorname{div}$.**
For $s,t\in\mathbb R$ and $u\in H^t$ define $\Lambda^s u\in H^{t-s}$ by the coefficient rule
$$\widehat{\Lambda^s u}(k):=w_k^{s}\,\widehat u(k);$$
then $\Lambda^s$ is a linear isometric isomorphism of $H^t$ onto $H^{t-s}$, $\Lambda^0=\mathrm{id}$, $\Lambda^s\Lambda^t=\Lambda^{s+t}$, and $\Lambda^{-s}$ is the inverse of $\Lambda^s$. For $j=1,2,3$ and $u\in H^{s+1}$ define $\partial_j u\in H^s$ by
$$\widehat{\partial_j u}(k):=2\pi i\,k_j\,\widehat u(k);$$
for $u\in H^{s+2}$ define $\Delta u\in H^s$ by $\widehat{\Delta u}(k):=-4\pi^2|k|_2^2\,\widehat u(k)$; for a scalar field $f$ with coefficients $\widehat f(k)\in\mathbb C$ in the scalar spaces just defined, define $\nabla f\in H^s$ for $f\in H^{s+1}$ by $\widehat{\nabla f}(k):=2\pi i\,k\,\widehat f(k)$; and for $u\in H^{s+1}$ define $\operatorname{div}u:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j u_j\in H^s$. These operators satisfy $\|\partial_j u\|_{H^s}\le\|u\|_{H^{s+1}}$, $\|\Delta u\|_{H^s}\le\|u\|_{H^{s+2}}$, and for every integer $m\ge1$, $\Lambda^{2m}=(I-\Delta)^m$, the identity following coefficientwise from $w_k^2=1+4\pi^2|k|_2^2$. On trigonometric polynomials all four operators agree with the classical coordinatewise derivatives and divergence computed from the smooth functions $x\mapsto e^{2\pi ik\cdot x}$, by the classical rules $\partial_j e_k=2\pi i k_j e_k$; this is the convention in which the notation is used below.

**Divergence-free fields and the Leray projection.** For $s\in\mathbb R$ put
$$H^s_\sigma(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3):=\bigl\{\,u\in H^s: k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0\ \text{for every }k\in\mathbb Z^3\,\bigr\};$$
this is a closed real-linear subspace of $H^s$, and $\operatorname{div}u=0$ in $H^s$ for $u\in H^{s+1}_\sigma$. For $k\neq0$ let $\pi_k\in L(\mathbb C^3)$ be the orthogonal projection onto the hyperplane $\{k\}^\perp$,
$$\pi_k v:=v-\frac{k\cdot v}{|k|_2^2}\,k ,$$
and set $\pi_0:=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C^3}$. Define the **Leray projection** $P$ by
$$\widehat{Pu}(k):=\pi_k\widehat u(k)\qquad(k\in\mathbb Z^3).$$
Then: $P$ maps $H^s$ linearly into $H^s_\sigma$, and $\|Pu\|_{H^s}\le\|u\|_{H^s}$; $P^2=P$; $P$ is self-adjoint on $H^s$, i.e. $\langle Pu,v\rangle_{H^s}=\langle u,Pv\rangle_{H^s}$ for all $u,v\in H^s$; $P$ commutes with each $\Lambda^t$, with each $\partial_j$, and with $\Delta$ wherever these are defined; and the identity $\operatorname{div}(Pu)=0$ holds in $H^{s-1}$ for $u\in H^s$. Moreover every $u\in H^s$ has the orthogonal decomposition
$$u=Pu+\nabla f,\qquad f\in H^{s+1},\quad \widehat f(0)=0,\qquad \langle Pu,\nabla f\rangle_{H^s}=0.$$
Here zero mean means zero coefficient at $0$ (the usual integral when the field is integrable); orthogonality for all real orders is in the $H^s$ pairing. The scalar element $f$ is determined by $\widehat f(0):=0$ and $\widehat f(k):=\dfrac{k\cdot\widehat u(k)}{2\pi i\,|k|_2^2}$ for $k\neq0$; here $f\in H^{s+1}$ because $w_k^{2(s+1)}|\widehat f(k)|^2\le C\,w_k^{2s}|\widehat u(k)|^2$ for $k\neq0$, and $\widehat{\nabla f}(k)=\bigl(k\cdot\widehat u(k)/|k|_2^2\bigr)k=\widehat u(k)-\pi_k\widehat u(k)$. In particular $P\nabla f=0$ for every $f$ with $\nabla f\in H^s$, so $P$ is the orthogonal projection of $H^s$ onto $H^s_\sigma$. On smooth fields the decomposition $u=Pu+\nabla f$ derived above from the Fourier coefficients is called the Hodge decomposition of the torus; the operator $P$ is the Leray projection of the fluid literature.

**Time-dependent fields.** For an interval $[0,T]$ with $T>0$ and $s\in\mathbb R$, let $C([0,T],H^s)$ denote the set of continuous maps from $[0,T]$ to the metric space $(H^s,\|\cdot\|_{H^s})$, with $\|u\|_{C([0,T],H^s)}:=\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|u(t)\|_{H^s}$. For a map $u:[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^\infty$ we mean that every mixed partial derivative $\partial_t^r\partial_x^\alpha u$ exists and is continuous on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3$, with one-sided time derivatives at $t=0,T$.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), as the Fourier-basis and measure-theoretic suppliers below do. Work with either the scalar spaces $H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R)$ or the vector spaces $H^s=H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and the weight family $w_k$ of [[def-periodic-vector-sobolev-space-and-leray-projection]]. In the scalar case replace $\mathbb R^3$ by $\mathbb R$ and vector norms by absolute values throughout. Let $\sigma>3/2$ and $u\in H^\sigma$.

1. **Continuous representative.** The coefficient series converges absolutely, $\sum_k|\widehat u(k)|_2\le W_\sigma\|u\|_{H^\sigma}$ with $W_\sigma$ as in [[lem-cm-lattice-shell-count-and-weight-sums]], and $S_M:=\sum_{|k|_\infty\le M}\widehat u(k)e_k$ converges uniformly on $\mathbb T^3$ to a continuous field $\widetilde u\in C(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ with the same Fourier coefficients, $\widehat{\widetilde u}(k)=\widehat u(k)$ for all $k$, which satisfies $\widetilde u=u$ almost everywhere and
$$\|\widetilde u\|_{L^\infty}=\sup_{x\in\mathbb T^3}|\widetilde u(x)|_2\;\le\;W_\sigma\|u\|_{H^\sigma}.$$
2. **Uniqueness of the continuous representative.** In the scalar case replace $\mathbb R^3$ by $\mathbb R$ in the following formulas. If $f,g\in C(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ satisfy $f=g$ almost everywhere, then $f=g$ everywhere. Consequently the field $\widetilde u$ is the only continuous field equal to $u$ almost everywhere, and if $u$ has a continuous representative $w$ then $\widetilde u=w$; in particular for $u\in C(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$, $\widetilde u=u$.
3. **Higher order.** If $j\ge0$ is an integer and $\sigma>j+3/2$, then the canonical representative $\widetilde u\in C^j$, and its classical derivatives are the corresponding uniform series
$$\partial^\alpha\widetilde u=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(2\pi i k)^\alpha\widehat u(k)\,e_k\qquad(|\alpha|\le j),$$
the series being absolutely and uniformly convergent, and
$$\|u\|_{C^j}:=\max_{|\alpha|\le j}\sup_{x\in\mathbb T^3}|\partial^\alpha\widetilde u(x)|_2\;\le\;C_{\sigma,j}\|u\|_{H^\sigma},\qquad C_{\sigma,j}:=\max_{|\alpha|\le j}W_{\sigma-|\alpha|}.$$
4. **Derivative bound for differentiable fields.** If $\sigma>3/2$, $u\in H^{\sigma+1}$ and $\partial_ju$ is continuous for some $j$, then $\partial_ju\in H^\sigma$ has continuous representative $\partial_ju$ itself and
$$\sup_{x\in\mathbb T^3}|\partial_ju(x)|_2\;\le\;W_\sigma\|\partial_ju\|_{H^\sigma}\;\le\;W_\sigma\|u\|_{H^{\sigma+1}}.$$

boundaries.evidence: The pressure-reconstruction Statement sums over the fixed three coordinate indices and the nonempty frequency lattice; the zero mode is separately assigned zero pressure coefficient.

The pressure definition assigns its zero-frequency value before division by frequency magnitude. At zero velocity the product coefficients vanish and the unique mean-zero pressure is zero by step 3.1.
The pressure coefficient formula applies to each individual nonzero frequency, and uniqueness in step 3.1 checks each such coefficient separately; no minimum number of supported modes is required.

The pressure multiplier coefficients k_i*k_j/|k| squared are bounded at every nonzero mode. Step 1.2 uses this bounded multiplier directly, without asserting an extra inverse-frequency decay that the numerator cancels.

The pressure-reconstruction Statement and step 1.2 use continuous all-order curves on the closed strip and the smoothness-bootstrap endpoint convention. The zero mode is included by the explicit definition, not by a limiting division.

boundaries.reason: The pressure is specified coefficientwise and uniquely by its zero mean. Step 3.1 proves uniqueness, so no selection of a pressure normalization over the time interval is required.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 substitutes the reconstructed gradient into the projected equation to obtain the primitive-variable system, supplying the forward reading of the pressure characterization.

If a mean-zero smooth scalar q makes the primitive system hold for this fixed u, subtracting the equations gives its gradient equal to that of p; step 3.1 forces q=p. This proves the reverse uniqueness reading stated after clause 3.

risk_review.notes: Scalar pressure now lives in the explicitly defined scalar H^m. Its k≠0 multiplier is bounded by the sum of nine product norms and preserves conjugate symmetry; k=0 is zero. Product bounds are used only above 3/2, and higher orders cover lower targets. The reviewed bootstrap supplies all time derivatives of u; bounded bilinear products and multiplier commute with these derivatives, yielding joint smoothness through scalar embedding. Computed every 2pi factor and sign: grad p=-(I-P)v and Delta p=-sum partial_i partial_j(u_i u_j). Injectivity yields equality almost everywhere, then positive-measure neighborhoods give equality everywhere. Constant velocities and zero u give p=0. No empirical premise enters.

so that $w_k\ge|2\pi k_j|$ for $j=1,2,3$ and $w_{k+l}\le w_k+w_l$ for all $k,l\in\mathbb Z^3$.

**The coefficient space and $H^s$.** For $s\in\mathbb R$ let $\ell^2_s$ be the complex Hilbert space of all $c:\mathbb Z^3\to\mathbb C^3$ with
$$\|c\|_{\ell^2_s}^2:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}w_k^{2s}|c(k)|_2^2<+\infty,\qquad \langle c,d\rangle_{\ell^2_s}:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}w_k^{2s}\,c(k)\cdot\overline{d(k)} ,$$
and let $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}:=\{c\in\ell^2_s: c(-k)=\overline{c(k)}\ \forall k\}$. The set $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$ is closed in $\ell^2_s$ and is a real-linear subspace; on it the Hermitian pairing $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\ell^2_s}$ is real valued, because the substitution $k\mapsto-k$ shows that it equals its own conjugate. By the imported theorem the coefficient map restricts to a bijection of the set of real classes of $L^2$ onto $\ell^2_{0,\mathbb R}$. For $s\ge0$ define
$$H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3):=\{u\in L^2:\widehat u\in\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}\},\qquad \|u\|_{H^s}:=\|\widehat u\|_{\ell^2_s}.$$
For $s<0$ define $H^s$ to be the completion of the real trigonometric polynomials in the same weighted coefficient norm, equivalently the space of formal real coefficient families $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$. For an element of this completion $\widehat u(k)$ means its coefficient, not an integral of an assumed $L^2$ function. The embedding of $L^2$ into these negative-order spaces is its coefficient map. Truncation makes finite families dense, so this completion is all of $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$, not merely the coefficient families of $L^2$ fields. Consequently each $H^s$ is a real Hilbert space isometric to $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$ through $u\mapsto\widehat u$, and $\|u\|_{H^0}=|u|_2$. If $s\ge t$ then $H^s\subseteq H^t$ and $\|u\|_{H^t}\le\|u\|_{H^s}$. The **trigonometric polynomials** are the fields $p=\sum_{k\in F}c_k e_k$ with $F\subseteq\mathbb Z^3$ finite and $c_{-k}=\overline{c_k}$ (equivalently, real coefficient families of finite support); they belong to every $H^s$, and the finitely supported families are dense in each $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$ (truncate a family to $|k|_\infty\le M$ and let $M\to\infty$), so trigonometric polynomials are dense in every $H^s$.

**Scalar spaces.** For $s\in\mathbb R$ define $\ell^2_s(\mathbb Z^3;\mathbb C)$ to consist of families $c:\mathbb Z^3\to\mathbb C$ with $\sum_k w_k^{2s}|c(k)|^2<\infty$, with pairing $\sum_k w_k^{2s}c(k)\overline{d(k)}$; its real subspace is specified by $c(-k)=\overline{c(k)}$. For $s\ge0$, $H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R)$ consists of real scalar $L^2$ classes with this weighted coefficient norm; for $s<0$ it is the completion of real scalar trigonometric polynomials, identified with the real coefficient subspace. Scalar Fourier coefficients are $\widehat f(k)=\int f e_{-k}\,dx$ when $f\in L^1$, and otherwise denote the completion coordinates. Parseval and truncation give the scalar Hilbert-space and density assertions exactly as above. A vector belongs to $H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ exactly when each of its three scalar components belongs to $H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R)$, with $\|u\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{j=1}^3\|u_j\|_{H^s}^2$. Below the value type distinguishes scalar and vector $H^s$; $\Lambda^s$, $\partial_j$ and $\Delta$ have the same multipliers for scalars, $\nabla$ maps scalar to vector spaces, and $\operatorname{div}$ maps vector to scalar spaces.

**The operators $\Lambda^s$, $\partial_j$, $\Delta$, $\nabla$ and $\operatorname{div}$.**
For $s,t\in\mathbb R$ and $u\in H^t$ define $\Lambda^s u\in H^{t-s}$ by the coefficient rule
$$\widehat{\Lambda^s u}(k):=w_k^{s}\,\widehat u(k);$$
then $\Lambda^s$ is a linear isometric isomorphism of $H^t$ onto $H^{t-s}$, $\Lambda^0=\mathrm{id}$, $\Lambda^s\Lambda^t=\Lambda^{s+t}$, and $\Lambda^{-s}$ is the inverse of $\Lambda^s$. For $j=1,2,3$ and $u\in H^{s+1}$ define $\partial_j u\in H^s$ by
$$\widehat{\partial_j u}(k):=2\pi i\,k_j\,\widehat u(k);$$
for $u\in H^{s+2}$ define $\Delta u\in H^s$ by $\widehat{\Delta u}(k):=-4\pi^2|k|_2^2\,\widehat u(k)$; for a scalar field $f$ with coefficients $\widehat f(k)\in\mathbb C$ in the scalar spaces just defined, define $\nabla f\in H^s$ for $f\in H^{s+1}$ by $\widehat{\nabla f}(k):=2\pi i\,k\,\widehat f(k)$; and for $u\in H^{s+1}$ define $\operatorname{div}u:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j u_j\in H^s$. These operators satisfy $\|\partial_j u\|_{H^s}\le\|u\|_{H^{s+1}}$, $\|\Delta u\|_{H^s}\le\|u\|_{H^{s+2}}$, and for every integer $m\ge1$, $\Lambda^{2m}=(I-\Delta)^m$, the identity following coefficientwise from $w_k^2=1+4\pi^2|k|_2^2$. On trigonometric polynomials all four operators agree with the classical coordinatewise derivatives and divergence computed from the smooth functions $x\mapsto e^{2\pi ik\cdot x}$, by the classical rules $\partial_j e_k=2\pi i k_j e_k$; this is the convention in which the notation is used below.

**Divergence-free fields and the Leray projection.** For $s\in\mathbb R$ put
$$H^s_\sigma(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3):=\bigl\{\,u\in H^s: k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0\ \text{for every }k\in\mathbb Z^3\,\bigr\};$$
this is a closed real-linear subspace of $H^s$, and $\operatorname{div}u=0$ in $H^s$ for $u\in H^{s+1}_\sigma$. For $k\neq0$ let $\pi_k\in L(\mathbb C^3)$ be the orthogonal projection onto the hyperplane $\{k\}^\perp$,
$$\pi_k v:=v-\frac{k\cdot v}{|k|_2^2}\,k ,$$
and set $\pi_0:=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C^3}$. Define the **Leray projection** $P$ by
$$\widehat{Pu}(k):=\pi_k\widehat u(k)\qquad(k\in\mathbb Z^3).$$
Then: $P$ maps $H^s$ linearly into $H^s_\sigma$, and $\|Pu\|_{H^s}\le\|u\|_{H^s}$; $P^2=P$; $P$ is self-adjoint on $H^s$, i.e. $\langle Pu,v\rangle_{H^s}=\langle u,Pv\rangle_{H^s}$ for all $u,v\in H^s$; $P$ commutes with each $\Lambda^t$, with each $\partial_j$, and with $\Delta$ wherever these are defined; and the identity $\operatorname{div}(Pu)=0$ holds in $H^{s-1}$ for $u\in H^s$. Moreover every $u\in H^s$ has the orthogonal decomposition
$$u=Pu+\nabla f,\qquad f\in H^{s+1},\quad \widehat f(0)=0,\qquad \langle Pu,\nabla f\rangle_{H^s}=0.$$
Here zero mean means zero coefficient at $0$ (the usual integral when the field is integrable); orthogonality for all real orders is in the $H^s$ pairing. The scalar element $f$ is determined by $\widehat f(0):=0$ and $\widehat f(k):=\dfrac{k\cdot\widehat u(k)}{2\pi i\,|k|_2^2}$ for $k\neq0$; here $f\in H^{s+1}$ because $w_k^{2(s+1)}|\widehat f(k)|^2\le C\,w_k^{2s}|\widehat u(k)|^2$ for $k\neq0$, and $\widehat{\nabla f}(k)=\bigl(k\cdot\widehat u(k)/|k|_2^2\bigr)k=\widehat u(k)-\pi_k\widehat u(k)$. In particular $P\nabla f=0$ for every $f$ with $\nabla f\in H^s$, so $P$ is the orthogonal projection of $H^s$ onto $H^s_\sigma$. On smooth fields the decomposition $u=Pu+\nabla f$ derived above from the Fourier coefficients is called the Hodge decomposition of the torus; the operator $P$ is the Leray projection of the fluid literature.

**Time-dependent fields.** For an interval $[0,T]$ with $T>0$ and $s\in\mathbb R$, let $C([0,T],H^s)$ denote the set of continuous maps from $[0,T]$ to the metric space $(H^s,\|\cdot\|_{H^s})$, with $\|u\|_{C([0,T],H^s)}:=\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|u(t)\|_{H^s}$. For a map $u:[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^\infty$ we mean that every mixed partial derivative $\partial_t^r\partial_x^\alpha u$ exists and is continuous on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3$, with one-sided time derivatives at $t=0,T$.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable, and let $E\in\mathcal A$. Since
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]
implies that $f\chi_E$ is measurable, define the **integral of $f$ over $E$**
by
$$\int_E f\,d\mu:=\int f\chi_E\,d\mu,$$
where the integral on the right is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), used through the lattice and embedding suppliers. Work with the operators $\Lambda^m$, $\partial_j$, the weight family $w_k$ and the divergence-free subspaces of [[def-periodic-vector-sobolev-space-and-leray-projection]].

1. **Vanishing transport integral.** Let $m>5/2$, let $u\in H^m$ with $\operatorname{div}u=0$, and let $w\in H^m$. Then $(u\cdot\nabla)w\in L^2$ and
$$\int_{\mathbb T^3}\bigl((u\cdot\nabla)w\bigr)\cdot w\,dx=0 .$$
2. **Tame commutator.** Let $m\ge s>5/2$ and $u\in H^m$ with $\operatorname{div}u=0$. Then the field
$$[\Lambda^m,u\cdot\nabla]u:=\Lambda^m\bigl((u\cdot\nabla)u\bigr)-(u\cdot\nabla)(\Lambda^m u)$$
belongs to $L^2$, and with $W'_s=(\sum_k(2\pi|k|_2)^2w_k^{-2s})^{1/2}$ of [[lem-cm-lattice-shell-count-and-weight-sums]] and $C_m:=4\pi^2m2^{m-2}(W'_s+1)$,
$$\bigl\|[\Lambda^m,u\cdot\nabla]u\bigr\|_{L^2}\;\le\;C_m\|u\|_{H^m}\|u\|_{H^s}.$$
3. **Commutation identity for the energy estimate.** If moreover $u\in H^{2m}$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$, then
$$\bigl\langle (u\cdot\nabla)u,\Lambda^{2m}u\bigr\rangle=\bigl\langle [\Lambda^m,u\cdot\nabla]u,\Lambda^mu\bigr\rangle,$$
where $\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{\mathbb T^3}f\cdot g\,dx$.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), as the Fourier-basis and measure-theoretic suppliers below do. Work with either the scalar spaces $H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R)$ or the vector spaces $H^s=H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and the weight family $w_k$ of [[def-periodic-vector-sobolev-space-and-leray-projection]]. In the scalar case replace $\mathbb R^3$ by $\mathbb R$ and vector norms by absolute values throughout. Let $\sigma>3/2$ and $u\in H^\sigma$.

1. **Continuous representative.** The coefficient series converges absolutely, $\sum_k|\widehat u(k)|_2\le W_\sigma\|u\|_{H^\sigma}$ with $W_\sigma$ as in [[lem-cm-lattice-shell-count-and-weight-sums]], and $S_M:=\sum_{|k|_\infty\le M}\widehat u(k)e_k$ converges uniformly on $\mathbb T^3$ to a continuous field $\widetilde u\in C(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ with the same Fourier coefficients, $\widehat{\widetilde u}(k)=\widehat u(k)$ for all $k$, which satisfies $\widetilde u=u$ almost everywhere and
$$\|\widetilde u\|_{L^\infty}=\sup_{x\in\mathbb T^3}|\widetilde u(x)|_2\;\le\;W_\sigma\|u\|_{H^\sigma}.$$
2. **Uniqueness of the continuous representative.** In the scalar case replace $\mathbb R^3$ by $\mathbb R$ in the following formulas. If $f,g\in C(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ satisfy $f=g$ almost everywhere, then $f=g$ everywhere. Consequently the field $\widetilde u$ is the only continuous field equal to $u$ almost everywhere, and if $u$ has a continuous representative $w$ then $\widetilde u=w$; in particular for $u\in C(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$, $\widetilde u=u$.
3. **Higher order.** If $j\ge0$ is an integer and $\sigma>j+3/2$, then the canonical representative $\widetilde u\in C^j$, and its classical derivatives are the corresponding uniform series
$$\partial^\alpha\widetilde u=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(2\pi i k)^\alpha\widehat u(k)\,e_k\qquad(|\alpha|\le j),$$
the series being absolutely and uniformly convergent, and
$$\|u\|_{C^j}:=\max_{|\alpha|\le j}\sup_{x\in\mathbb T^3}|\partial^\alpha\widetilde u(x)|_2\;\le\;C_{\sigma,j}\|u\|_{H^\sigma},\qquad C_{\sigma,j}:=\max_{|\alpha|\le j}W_{\sigma-|\alpha|}.$$
4. **Derivative bound for differentiable fields.** If $\sigma>3/2$, $u\in H^{\sigma+1}$ and $\partial_ju$ is continuous for some $j$, then $\partial_ju\in H^\sigma$ has continuous representative $\partial_ju$ itself and
$$\sup_{x\in\mathbb T^3}|\partial_ju(x)|_2\;\le\;W_\sigma\|\partial_ju\|_{H^\sigma}\;\le\;W_\sigma\|u\|_{H^{\sigma+1}}.$$

Let $p,q>1$ with $1/p+1/q=1$. For real families $(a_i)_{i<n}$ and $(b_i)_{i<n}$,
$$\sum_{i<n}|a_ib_i|\le\left(\sum_{i<n}|a_i|^p\right)^{1/p}\left(\sum_{i<n}|b_i|^q\right)^{1/q}.$$

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), which is used by the imported Fourier-basis theorem quoted below.

**The three-torus and its measure.** Let $\mathbb T:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the one-dimensional torus with its quotient topology and its normalized Haar integral $m_{\mathbb T}$ ([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]); $\mathbb T$ is compact Hausdorff ([[lem-finite-tori-are-compact-hausdorff-character-spaces]]). Put $\mathbb T^3:=\mathbb T\times\mathbb T\times\mathbb T$ with the finite product topology. Let $dx:=m_{\mathbb T}\otimes m_{\mathbb T}\otimes m_{\mathbb T}$ be the product measure on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb T^3$ ([[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]], [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]); being a product of probability measures it is a probability measure. For a vector $k=(k_1,k_2,k_3)\in\mathbb Z^3$ and $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in\mathbb T^3$ define the **character**
$$e_k(x):=\exp\bigl(2\pi i\,(k_1x_1+k_2x_2+k_3x_3)\bigr)=e^{2\pi i\,k\cdot x},$$
where each $x_j$ is inserted through any real representative and $\exp$ is the complex exponential ([[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]); the definition does not depend on the representatives. Then $|e_k(x)|=1$, $e_k e_l=e_{k+l}$, and $e_{-k}=\overline{e_k}$.

**Function spaces.** Write $L^2:=L^2(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ for the real Hilbert space of (equivalence classes of) real Borel vector fields $u:\mathbb T^3\to\mathbb R^3$ with $\int_{\mathbb T^3}|u|_2^2\,dx<+\infty$, inner product $\langle u,v\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb T^3}u\cdot v\,dx$ and norm $|u|_2:=\langle u,u\rangle^{1/2}$; here $u\cdot v$ is the Euclidean inner product of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Similarly $L^1(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb C^3)$ denotes the integrable complex vector fields.

**Fourier coefficients.** For $u\in L^1(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb C^3)$ and $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ define
$$\widehat u(k):=\int_{\mathbb T^3}u(x)\,e_{-k}(x)\,dx\ \in\mathbb C^3 .$$
The integral depends only on the class of $u$. A field $u\in L^1$ is real almost everywhere if and only if $\widehat u(-k)=\overline{\widehat u(k)}$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z^3$; the forward direction uses $\widehat{\overline u}(k)=\overline{\widehat u(-k)}$, and the reverse uses $L^1$ Fourier uniqueness, proved below. On the circle this uniqueness follows from [[thm-fejer-convergence-in-lp]] with $p=1$: zero coefficients give zero Fejer means, whose $L^1$ limit is the function. To pass to $\mathbb T^d$ for $d=2,3$, use [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: for fixed $k'\in\mathbb Z^{d-1}$, $g_{k'}(x_1)=\int_{\mathbb T^{d-1}}u(x_1,x')e_{-k'}(x')dx'$ is in $L^1(\mathbb T)$ and all its coefficients vanish. Hence $g_{k'}=0$ almost everywhere. The countable union of the exceptional sets over $k'$ is null. For every remaining $x_1$, the $L^1$ section in $x'$ has all coefficients zero, so induction in $d$ makes it zero almost everywhere. Fubini then makes $u=0$ almost everywhere on $\mathbb T^d$. Apply this uniqueness to $u-\overline u$ to obtain the reverse real-valuedness implication. For $u\in L^2\subset L^1$ (finite measure) the coefficient map is the one of the imported theorem, which states: $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}$ is an orthonormal basis of the complex Hilbert space $L^2(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb C)$, the finite-subset-net expansion $u=\sum_k\widehat u(k)e_k$ and the Parseval identities hold, and $u\mapsto\widehat u$ is a surjective linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb C)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^3;\mathbb C)$ ([[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]]); the last statement applied componentwise gives $\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_k\widehat u(k)\cdot\overline{\widehat v(k)}$ for real $u,v\in L^2$.

**Weights.** For $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ set
$$w_k:=\bigl(1+|2\pi k|_2^2\bigr)^{1/2}=\bigl(1+4\pi^2|k|_2^2\bigr)^{1/2}\ \ge 1,$$
so that $w_k\ge|2\pi k_j|$ for $j=1,2,3$ and $w_{k+l}\le w_k+w_l$ for all $k,l\in\mathbb Z^3$.

**The coefficient space and $H^s$.** For $s\in\mathbb R$ let $\ell^2_s$ be the complex Hilbert space of all $c:\mathbb Z^3\to\mathbb C^3$ with
$$\|c\|_{\ell^2_s}^2:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}w_k^{2s}|c(k)|_2^2<+\infty,\qquad \langle c,d\rangle_{\ell^2_s}:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}w_k^{2s}\,c(k)\cdot\overline{d(k)} ,$$
and let $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}:=\{c\in\ell^2_s: c(-k)=\overline{c(k)}\ \forall k\}$. The set $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$ is closed in $\ell^2_s$ and is a real-linear subspace; on it the Hermitian pairing $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\ell^2_s}$ is real valued, because the substitution $k\mapsto-k$ shows that it equals its own conjugate. By the imported theorem the coefficient map restricts to a bijection of the set of real classes of $L^2$ onto $\ell^2_{0,\mathbb R}$. For $s\ge0$ define
$$H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3):=\{u\in L^2:\widehat u\in\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}\},\qquad \|u\|_{H^s}:=\|\widehat u\|_{\ell^2_s}.$$
For $s<0$ define $H^s$ to be the completion of the real trigonometric polynomials in the same weighted coefficient norm, equivalently the space of formal real coefficient families $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$. For an element of this completion $\widehat u(k)$ means its coefficient, not an integral of an assumed $L^2$ function. The embedding of $L^2$ into these negative-order spaces is its coefficient map. Truncation makes finite families dense, so this completion is all of $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$, not merely the coefficient families of $L^2$ fields. Consequently each $H^s$ is a real Hilbert space isometric to $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$ through $u\mapsto\widehat u$, and $\|u\|_{H^0}=|u|_2$. If $s\ge t$ then $H^s\subseteq H^t$ and $\|u\|_{H^t}\le\|u\|_{H^s}$. The **trigonometric polynomials** are the fields $p=\sum_{k\in F}c_k e_k$ with $F\subseteq\mathbb Z^3$ finite and $c_{-k}=\overline{c_k}$ (equivalently, real coefficient families of finite support); they belong to every $H^s$, and the finitely supported families are dense in each $\ell^2_{s,\mathbb R}$ (truncate a family to $|k|_\infty\le M$ and let $M\to\infty$), so trigonometric polynomials are dense in every $H^s$.

**Scalar spaces.** For $s\in\mathbb R$ define $\ell^2_s(\mathbb Z^3;\mathbb C)$ to consist of families $c:\mathbb Z^3\to\mathbb C$ with $\sum_k w_k^{2s}|c(k)|^2<\infty$, with pairing $\sum_k w_k^{2s}c(k)\overline{d(k)}$; its real subspace is specified by $c(-k)=\overline{c(k)}$. For $s\ge0$, $H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R)$ consists of real scalar $L^2$ classes with this weighted coefficient norm; for $s<0$ it is the completion of real scalar trigonometric polynomials, identified with the real coefficient subspace. Scalar Fourier coefficients are $\widehat f(k)=\int f e_{-k}\,dx$ when $f\in L^1$, and otherwise denote the completion coordinates. Parseval and truncation give the scalar Hilbert-space and density assertions exactly as above. A vector belongs to $H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ exactly when each of its three scalar components belongs to $H^s(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R)$, with $\|u\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{j=1}^3\|u_j\|_{H^s}^2$. Below the value type distinguishes scalar and vector $H^s$; $\Lambda^s$, $\partial_j$ and $\Delta$ have the same multipliers for scalars, $\nabla$ maps scalar to vector spaces, and $\operatorname{div}$ maps vector to scalar spaces.

**The operators $\Lambda^s$, $\partial_j$, $\Delta$, $\nabla$ and $\operatorname{div}$.**
For $s,t\in\mathbb R$ and $u\in H^t$ define $\Lambda^s u\in H^{t-s}$ by the coefficient rule
$$\widehat{\Lambda^s u}(k):=w_k^{s}\,\widehat u(k);$$
then $\Lambda^s$ is a linear isometric isomorphism of $H^t$ onto $H^{t-s}$, $\Lambda^0=\mathrm{id}$, $\Lambda^s\Lambda^t=\Lambda^{s+t}$, and $\Lambda^{-s}$ is the inverse of $\Lambda^s$. For $j=1,2,3$ and $u\in H^{s+1}$ define $\partial_j u\in H^s$ by
$$\widehat{\partial_j u}(k):=2\pi i\,k_j\,\widehat u(k);$$
for $u\in H^{s+2}$ define $\Delta u\in H^s$ by $\widehat{\Delta u}(k):=-4\pi^2|k|_2^2\,\widehat u(k)$; for a scalar field $f$ with coefficients $\widehat f(k)\in\mathbb C$ in the scalar spaces just defined, define $\nabla f\in H^s$ for $f\in H^{s+1}$ by $\widehat{\nabla f}(k):=2\pi i\,k\,\widehat f(k)$; and for $u\in H^{s+1}$ define $\operatorname{div}u:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j u_j\in H^s$. These operators satisfy $\|\partial_j u\|_{H^s}\le\|u\|_{H^{s+1}}$, $\|\Delta u\|_{H^s}\le\|u\|_{H^{s+2}}$, and for every integer $m\ge1$, $\Lambda^{2m}=(I-\Delta)^m$, the identity following coefficientwise from $w_k^2=1+4\pi^2|k|_2^2$. On trigonometric polynomials all four operators agree with the classical coordinatewise derivatives and divergence computed from the smooth functions $x\mapsto e^{2\pi ik\cdot x}$, by the classical rules $\partial_j e_k=2\pi i k_j e_k$; this is the convention in which the notation is used below.

**Divergence-free fields and the Leray projection.** For $s\in\mathbb R$ put
$$H^s_\sigma(\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3):=\bigl\{\,u\in H^s: k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0\ \text{for every }k\in\mathbb Z^3\,\bigr\};$$
this is a closed real-linear subspace of $H^s$, and $\operatorname{div}u=0$ in $H^s$ for $u\in H^{s+1}_\sigma$. For $k\neq0$ let $\pi_k\in L(\mathbb C^3)$ be the orthogonal projection onto the hyperplane $\{k\}^\perp$,
$$\pi_k v:=v-\frac{k\cdot v}{|k|_2^2}\,k ,$$
and set $\pi_0:=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C^3}$. Define the **Leray projection** $P$ by
$$\widehat{Pu}(k):=\pi_k\widehat u(k)\qquad(k\in\mathbb Z^3).$$
Then: $P$ maps $H^s$ linearly into $H^s_\sigma$, and $\|Pu\|_{H^s}\le\|u\|_{H^s}$; $P^2=P$; $P$ is self-adjoint on $H^s$, i.e. $\langle Pu,v\rangle_{H^s}=\langle u,Pv\rangle_{H^s}$ for all $u,v\in H^s$; $P$ commutes with each $\Lambda^t$, with each $\partial_j$, and with $\Delta$ wherever these are defined; and the identity $\operatorname{div}(Pu)=0$ holds in $H^{s-1}$ for $u\in H^s$. Moreover every $u\in H^s$ has the orthogonal decomposition
$$u=Pu+\nabla f,\qquad f\in H^{s+1},\quad \widehat f(0)=0,\qquad \langle Pu,\nabla f\rangle_{H^s}=0.$$
Here zero mean means zero coefficient at $0$ (the usual integral when the field is integrable); orthogonality for all real orders is in the $H^s$ pairing. The scalar element $f$ is determined by $\widehat f(0):=0$ and $\widehat f(k):=\dfrac{k\cdot\widehat u(k)}{2\pi i\,|k|_2^2}$ for $k\neq0$; here $f\in H^{s+1}$ because $w_k^{2(s+1)}|\widehat f(k)|^2\le C\,w_k^{2s}|\widehat u(k)|^2$ for $k\neq0$, and $\widehat{\nabla f}(k)=\bigl(k\cdot\widehat u(k)/|k|_2^2\bigr)k=\widehat u(k)-\pi_k\widehat u(k)$. In particular $P\nabla f=0$ for every $f$ with $\nabla f\in H^s$, so $P$ is the orthogonal projection of $H^s$ onto $H^s_\sigma$. On smooth fields the decomposition $u=Pu+\nabla f$ derived above from the Fourier coefficients is called the Hodge decomposition of the torus; the operator $P$ is the Leray projection of the fluid literature.

**Time-dependent fields.** For an interval $[0,T]$ with $T>0$ and $s\in\mathbb R$, let $C([0,T],H^s)$ denote the set of continuous maps from $[0,T]$ to the metric space $(H^s,\|\cdot\|_{H^s})$, with $\|u\|_{C([0,T],H^s)}:=\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|u(t)\|_{H^s}$. For a map $u:[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^\infty$ we mean that every mixed partial derivative $\partial_t^r\partial_x^\alpha u$ exists and is continuous on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3$, with one-sided time derivatives at $t=0,T$.

derivations.claim: Part (a): the coefficients of $\varphi$ are $\widehat\varphi(0,0,0)=0$ and, for the cosine term, $\widehat\varphi(\pm e_1)=\tfrac12$; for the sine term, $\widehat\varphi(e_2+e_3)=\tfrac{1}{2i}$ and $\widehat\varphi(-e_2-e_3)=-\tfrac{1}{2i}$. Hence $\widehat v(k)=2\pi ik\widehat\varphi(k)$ is a vector parallel to $k$ at every frequency (zero at frequency $0$), and the orthogonal projection $\pi_k$ kills it: for $k\ne0$, $\pi_k\bigl(2\pi ik\widehat\varphi(k)\bigr)=2\pi i\widehat\varphi(k)\bigl(1-\tfrac{k\cdot k}{|k|_2^2}\bigr)k=0$. Thus $Pv=0$, and $v=Pv+\nabla\varphi$ is the Hodge decomposition with zero divergence-free part.

Part (b): the coefficients of $u$ are supported on $k=\pm e_2$ (first component $1/(2i)$ and $-1/(2i)$) and $k=\pm e_3$ (third component $1/2$ and $1/2$). For $k=e_2$: $\widehat u(e_2)=(1/(2i),0,0)$ and $k\cdot\widehat u(e_2)=0$, so $\pi_k\widehat u=\widehat u$; for $k=-e_2$ likewise. For $k=e_3$: $\widehat u(e_3)=(0,0,1/2)$ and $k\cdot\widehat u(e_3)=1/2$, so $\pi_k\widehat u=\widehat u-\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot\tfrac{1}{1}(0,0,1)=(0,0,0)$; for $k=-e_3$: $\widehat u=(0,0,1/2)$, $k\cdot\widehat u=-1/2$ and $\pi_k\widehat u=(0,0,1/2)-\tfrac{-1/2}{1}(0,0,-1)=(0,0,0)$. Hence $Pu=(\sin(2\pi x_2),0,0)$; moreover $\nabla f$ for $f=\tfrac1{2\pi}\sin(2\pi x_3)$ has coefficients $2\pi i k\widehat f(k)$ equal to $(0,0,1/2)$ at $k=e_3$ and $(0,0,1/2)$ at $k=-e_3$, which is exactly $u-Pu$, so $u-Pu=\nabla f$ is a gradient field.

Part (b), orthogonality and norms: since $\sin(2\pi x_2)$ and $\cos(2\pi x_3)$ are functions of different coordinates, $\langle Pu,u-Pu\rangle=\int_{\mathbb T^3}\sin(2\pi x_2)\cdot0+0\cdot0+0\cdot\cos(2\pi x_3)\,dx=0$; and $\int_0^1\sin^2(2\pi s)ds=\int_0^1\cos^2(2\pi s)ds=\tfrac12$, so $\|Pu\|_{L^2}^2=\tfrac12$, $\|u-Pu\|_{L^2}^2=\tfrac12$, and $\|u\|_{L^2}^2=1$ (the mixed terms vanish by separation of variables). This verifies the orthogonal decomposition identity of [[def-periodic-vector-sobolev-space-and-leray-projection]] on this example.

Part (c): for each $k'\in\mathbb Z^3$, $\widehat u(k')=\tfrac{1}{2i}A$ if $k'=k$, $-\tfrac{1}{2i}A$ if $k'=-k$, and $0$ otherwise; since $A\cdot k=0$, $k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0$ and $\pi_k\widehat u(k)=\widehat u(k)$ (and likewise at $-k$), so $Pu=u$. The divergence has coefficients $2\pi i(k'\cdot\widehat u(k'))=0$ at $k'=\pm k$, so $\operatorname{div}u=0$; and for any $v\in H^0$ the pairing $\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_{k'}\widehat u(k')\cdot\overline{\widehat v(k')}$ only involves $k'=\pm k$ where $\widehat u\perp k'$, so it equals the pairing of $u$ with $Pv$ because $(I-P)v$ has coefficients parallel to $k'$ there: $\widehat u(\pm k)\cdot\overline{(I-P)v(\pm k)}=0$.
